 Why South Korean actors are playing European royalty in K-drama’s new fantasy trend Why South Korean actors are playing European royalty in K-drama’s new fantasy trend
 From “The Remarried Empress” to “Men of the Harem,” popular web novels and webtoons bring European-inspired palace fantasy to Korean screens.
 Lee Yoon-seo
 The Korea Herald
View all posts by Lee Yoon-seo → 
 "The Remarried Empress," starring Shin Min-a (left) and Lee Jong-suk PHOTO: DISNEY+/THE KOREA HERALD
 November 19, 2026
 SEOUL – Their world is one of glittering tiaras, extravagant ball gowns and sprawling European castles. Surrounded by royal courts, aristocratic intrigue and forbidden romance, these characters look as though they stepped out of a Western period fantasy — except they are played by Korean actors speaking Korean.
 This unlikely fusion of Korean drama and European fantasy is emerging as K-drama’s next big genre.
 Long considered too expensive to produce and culturally unfamiliar to domestic audiences, romantasy — a blend of romance and fantasy — is gaining ground on South Korean television, driven by the growing popularity of web novels and webtoons that have already built a devoted following for the genre.
 For decades, Korean television largely steered clear of Western-style fantasy. Local fantasy series favored contemporary Korean settings laced with supernatural elements, while period dramas mined domestic history, spanning the Joseon, Goryeo and Three Kingdoms eras. Full-scale ventures into Western-inspired romance remained virtually nonexistent.
 Hefty production budgets have historically been a major deterrent.
 Mounting a Western-style romantasy requires heavy spending on production design and set construction, often outpacing modern-day series or traditional “sageuk” (Korean historical dramas). Building imperial palaces and grand ballrooms demands elaborate, bespoke Western sets, while period-inspired gowns and royal regalia drive up costume budgets, leaving Korean studios reluctant to take the financial gamble.
 Cultural unfamiliarity has posed another hurdle.
 Korean historical dramas have long drawn on Korea’s traditional social hierarchies and royal court intrigues; Western-style series, by contrast, demand establishing an unfamiliar socio-political framework from the ground up. Viewers must navigate an unfamiliar system of Western nobility, from dukes and marquesses to counts.
 Yet the massive built-in readership for similarly styled web novels and webtoons, paired with the breakout success of Disney+’s live adaptation of “The Remarried Empress,” is turning the genre into a lucrative new frontier for streamers and networks alike.
 Netflix is currently producing “Men of the Harem,” slated for next year. Adapted from the smash-hit web novel of the same name, the palace romantasy centers on Latil, empress of the Tarium empire, who establishes a harem of male consorts to shore up her grip on the throne.
 The series has assembled an A-list creative roster. Lee Eung-bok — the helmer behind megahits “Descendants of the Sun,” “Guardian: The Lonely and Great God,” “Mr. Sunshine,” and Netflix’s “Sweet Home” — is directing, working from scripts by “My Dearest” scribe Hwang Jin-young. Bae Suzy (“Doona!,” “Genie, Make A Wish”) headlines as Empress Latil, rounded out by an ensemble cast featuring Shin Seung-ho, Dex (Kim Jin-young), Kim Dan and Yoo Jung-hoo.
 Another heavyweight intellectual property, “I’m the Queen in This Life,” is also bound for the small screen. Originally serialized on Naver in 2020 as a web novel before launching as a webtoon in 2022, the smash-hit revenge drama follows Ariadne, a woman betrayed by her fiance, older sister, and parents. After being sent 15 years back in time, she plots her vengeance and fights to claim the crown in the Etruscan Kingdom.
 “Mr. Sunshine” and “The Handmaiden” star Kim Tae-ri is reportedly in talks to headline, with hit JTBC series “Reborn Rich” director Jung Dae-yoon attached to direct.
